issues.legal_issue: A successor’s suit to recover occupancy land is barred when the landowner has obtained exclusive possession under eviction decrees and that possession has continued beyond the limitation period, whether or not the former manager represented the institution.
material_facts: The land was held under an occupancy tenancy, although it was disputed whether the tenant was the religious institution or its manager.
The landowner obtained eviction decrees and took possession of the land.
The landowner remained in exclusive physical possession for more than twelve years before the successor manager brought the recovery suit.
issues.conclusion: The occupancy right merged into the landowner’s ownership upon eviction; independently, the exclusive possession for more than twelve years extinguished the occupancy right. The successor’s suit was barred by limitation.
issues.legal_principle: Under the limitation principle reflected in Article 144 of the Limitation Act, adverse possession is computed from effective possession. A manager represents the religious institution, and if the former manager represented it, the decrees bind the successor; if not, possession obtained under those decrees is adverse to the institution. The Court applied Sudarsan Das v. Ram Kirpal and Subbaiya v. Mustapha.

rule.if: successor_recovery_suit and eviction_order_for_tenant and owner_exclusive_possession_beyond_limitation_period and suit_filed_after_limitation_period

predicates.successor_recovery_suit: A successor to the manager of an institution brings a suit to recover land claimed for the institution.
predicates.eviction_order_for_tenant: A landowner obtains an order evicting the person or institution holding the land as an occupancy tenant.
predicates.owner_exclusive_possession_beyond_limita: The landowner holds the land in physical possession to the exclusion of the occupancy claimant for longer than the applicable limitation period.
predicates.suit_filed_after_limitation_period: The successor brings the recovery suit after the applicable limitation period has elapsed from the start of the landowner’s possession.

issues.definition: When a successor brings a recovery suit after the landowner has obtained an eviction order and held the land exclusively beyond the limitation period, the occupancy recovery claim is time-barred.

issues.legal_issue: A landowner’s forfeiture of an occupancy tenancy for breach is not an alienation by the tenant that gives the tenant’s successor a fresh limitation period upon succeeding to management.
material_facts: The tenant’s lessee dug up the land for brick manufacture.
The landowner obtained eviction decrees on the basis of the conduct relating to the land and took possession.
The successor argued that the former manager’s conduct was an unauthorised alienation and that time should run from the successor’s appointment.
issues.conclusion: The eviction was a forfeiture of the occupancy tenancy by the landowner, not a voluntary alienation by the former manager; succession to the management did not make the suit timely.
issues.legal_principle: Alienation is a voluntary act by a transferor in favour of a transferee. The landowner’s enforcement of forfeiture is not such a transfer, and the successor could not rely on the limitation argument applicable to a claim based on the manager’s alienation.

rule.if: successor_recovery_suit and landlord_evicted_tenant_for_breach and no_voluntary_transfer_by_tenant and successor_relies_on_alienation_to_restart_limitation

predicates.successor_recovery_suit: A successor to the manager brings a suit to recover land claimed for the institution.
predicates.landlord_evicted_tenant_for_breach: The landowner obtains eviction of the tenant because of conduct constituting a breach of the tenancy conditions.
predicates.no_voluntary_transfer_by_tenant: The tenant did not voluntarily transfer the tenancy or land to another person.
predicates.successor_relies_on_alienation_to_restar: The successor argues that the former manager’s conduct was an alienation and that limitation began anew upon the successor’s appointment.

issues.definition: If a successor seeks to restart limitation based on an alleged alienation, but the landowner evicted the tenant for breach and the tenant made no voluntary transfer, the eviction is forfeiture rather than alienation and successorship does not restart limitation.

issues.legal_issue: A gap between managers does not postpone the start of limitation when a person competent to sue for the institution could bring the recovery action during that period.
material_facts: The former manager remained in office until his removal, and a receiver was also appointed in the related proceedings.
The successor argued that adverse possession could not begin until the successor was appointed because no one could sue for the institution before then.
The Court held that the former manager could have sued on the institution’s behalf and that the receiver was legally competent to sue while in possession.
issues.conclusion: The limitation period was not postponed until the successor’s appointment because a competent person could have brought suit for the institution earlier.
issues.legal_principle: Limitation does not wait for a later manager’s appointment where a person capable of suing for the claimant already exists. The Court distinguished Dwijendra Narain Roy v. Joges Chandra De, whose observations had been approved in F. Lakshmi Reddy v. L. Lakshmi Reddy, because a competent representative was available in this case.

rule.if: successor_recovery_suit and adverse_possession_during_management_gap and (incumbent_manager_could_sue_for_institution or receiver_could_sue_for_institution)

predicates.successor_recovery_suit: A successor to an institution’s manager brings a suit to recover property for the institution.
predicates.adverse_possession_during_management_gap: The defendant possesses the property adversely to the institution during a period before the successor assumes management.
predicates.incumbent_manager_could_sue_for_institut: The incumbent manager remained able to bring a suit on the institution’s behalf during that period.
predicates.receiver_could_sue_for_institution: A receiver in possession during that period was legally able to bring a suit for the institution.

issues.definition: If adverse possession continues during a management gap and either the incumbent manager or a receiver could sue for the institution, limitation is not postponed until the successor’s appointment.
